scenario_meta.title: Checkout 500s after the 14:02 deploy
scenario_meta.summary: Customers report errors when placing orders; the checkout error budget is burning.

evidence.summary: medium alert slo_burn_rate_fast on checkout-service (value 0.09281)
incident INC-0117: checkout-service: 5xx spike after release 2026.01.25.5. error_rate 9% -> 24% within 8 min of deploy 2026.01.14.2; new ex

lessons: Roll back only the component that changed; rolling back neighbours changes nothing

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

agent_runs.summary: At 14:04 UTC, checkout errors jumped from a 0.29% baseline to 9.61% by 14:11, while p95 latency rose from 184 ms to 685 ms, breaching its 400 ms SLO. Cart and payments errors remained near baseline (0.164% vs 0.19%; 0.281% vs 0.35%); 10 alerts fired across checkout, edge, and web, supporting a checkout-centered issue with upstream impact rather than a broad cart or payments failure.

In the 30-minute window, checkout-service logged 20 WARN+ events: 16 errors and 4 warnings. The earlier baseline was one retried-and-succeeded 500 and two upstream timeout retries; from 14:05:01Z, circuit-breaker warnings reported 1,189, then 6,430 consecutive failures, while six `/v2/checkout` 500s and nine `OrderMapper.map` null-item exceptions appeared between 14:05:15Z and 14:10:03Z. This points toward a checkout

In the 240-minute window, the change log shows **one checkout-service change**: version 2026.11.05.2 deployed at **14:02 UTC**, nine minutes before the 14:11 snapshot. Its summary mentions express-checkout address validation, making the deploy a candidate cause, but no symptom onset or baseline was provided to test the timing. The record also conflicts on commit count (**9** in the summary, **7** in details).

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

agent_runs.summary: At 14:04 UTC, checkout errors jumped from a 0.29% baseline to 9.61% by 14:11, while p95 latency rose from 184 ms to 685 ms, breaching its 400 ms SLO. Cart and payments errors remained near baseline (0.164% vs 0.19%; 0.281% vs 0.35%); 10 alerts fired across checkout, edge, and web, supporting a checkout-centered issue with upstream impact rather than a broad cart or payments failure.

In the 30-minute window, checkout-service logged 20 WARN+ events: 16 errors and 4 warnings. The earlier baseline was one retried-and-succeeded 500 and two upstream timeout retries; from 14:05:01Z, circuit-breaker warnings reported 1,189, then 6,430 consecutive failures, while six `/v2/checkout` 500s and nine `OrderMapper.map` null-item exceptions appeared between 14:05:15Z and 14:10:03Z. This points toward a checkout

In the 240-minute window, the change log shows **one checkout-service change**: version 2026.11.05.2 deployed at **14:02 UTC**, nine minutes before the 14:11 snapshot. Its summary mentions express-checkout address validation, making the deploy a candidate cause, but no symptom onset or baseline was provided to test the timing. The record also conflicts on commit count (**9** in the summary, **7** in details).

# Postmortem INC-33721: INC-33721 (SEV2): checkout-service deploy caused checkout errors

*SEV2 - component `checkout-service` - revision 1 - draft*

## Summary
On November 5, INC-33721 was a 12-minute, customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway; eight alerts fired, including a checkout-service error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×). The incident commander identified the faulty checkout-service release as the root cause: it deployed at 14:02 UTC, the first alert fired at 14:06, a status update was posted and the deploy was rolled back at 14:11, and checkout-service recovered at 14:18; the specific code-level mechanism was not established. Follow-up actions are to add a canary stage and automatic rollback (j.okafor), alert on the first post-deploy error-rate increase (t.kowalski), and document the rollback decision in the runbook (s.whitfield).

## Impact
Customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway for 12 minutes; service recovered. Eight alerts fired across the two components. The initial checkout-service SLO burn-rate alert reported an error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×); a subsequent checkout-service error-rate alert reported 0.09441 against 0.02. The alert data do not quantify affected customers or transactions.

## Detection
The first recorded incident alert was checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast at 2026-11-05T14:06:00Z, four minutes after its deploy, with error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147. Additional checkout-service and edge-gateway error-rate and latency alerts followed.

## Root cause
The incident commander's assessment identifies a faulty release to checkout-service (deploy 2026.11.05.2, change:chg-check-9247) as the root-cause component and change. Supporting references are the checkout-service error-rate metric, the deploy change, and a checkout-service NullPointerException log. The facts do not establish a more specific code-level mechanism.

### Contributing factors
- The checkout-service release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- There was no automatic rollback on error-rate regression.

## Timeline (virtual time, UTC)
- * `2026-11-05T14:02:00Z` [change] deploybot deployed checkout-service release 2026.11.05.2 (9 commits: express checkout address validation).
- * `2026-11-05T14:06:00Z` [detection] checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service error_rate_high fired: 0.09441 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_high fired: 659.54 ms versus threshold 400 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.07258 versus threshold 0.008.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway error_rate_high fired: 0.07104 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_high fired: 482.21 ms versus threshold 200 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:09:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_degraded fired: 670.48 ms versus threshold 300 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:10:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_degraded fired: 474.99 ms versus threshold 150 ms.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Posted a status update.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Rolled back the checkout-service deploy.
- * `2026-11-05T14:18:00Z` [recovery] checkout-service recovered.

## What went well
- The checkout-service burn-rate alert detected the regression four minutes after the deploy.
- The team posted a status update and rolled back checkout-service; recovery was recorded seven minutes after rollback.

## What went badly
- The release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- No automatic rollback was in place for an error-rate regression.

## Action items
- [p0] Add a canary stage and automatic rollback on error-rate regression for checkout-service - owner: j.okafor (prevent)
- [p1] Alert on the first error-rate increase after every checkout-service deploy - owner: t.kowalski (detect)
- [p2] Document the rollback decision in the checkout-service runbook - owner: s.whitfield (process)

## Lessons learned
- Check the deploy time against the first error-rate increase, then roll back only the component that changed.

The incident commander identified the faulty checkout-service release as the root cause: it deployed at 14:02 UTC, the first alert fired at 14:06, a status update was posted and the deploy was rolled back at 14:11, and checkout-service recovered at 14:18; the specific code-level mechanism was not established. ## Impact
Customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway for 12 minutes; service recovered. Eight alerts fired across the two components. The initial checkout-service SLO burn-rate alert reported an error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×); a subsequent checkout-service error-rate alert reported 0.09441 against 0.02. The alert data do not quantify affected customers or transactions.

## Detection
The first recorded incident alert was checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast at 2026-11-05T14:06:00Z, four minutes after its deploy, with error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147. Additional checkout-service and edge-gateway error-rate and latency alerts followed.

## Root cause
The incident commander's assessment identifies a faulty release to checkout-service (deploy 2026.11.05.2, change:chg-check-9247) as the root-cause component and change. Supporting references are the checkout-service error-rate metric, the deploy change, and a checkout-service NullPointerException log. The facts do not establish a more specific code-level mechanism.

- The checkout-service release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- There was no automatic rollback on error-rate regression.

# Postmortem INC-33721: INC-33721 (SEV2): checkout-service deploy caused checkout errors

*SEV2 - component `checkout-service` - revision 1 - approved*

## Summary
On November 5, INC-33721 was a 12-minute, customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway; eight alerts fired, including a checkout-service error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×). The incident commander identified the faulty checkout-service release as the root cause: it deployed at 14:02 UTC, the first alert fired at 14:06, a status update was posted and the deploy was rolled back at 14:11, and checkout-service recovered at 14:18; the specific code-level mechanism was not established. Follow-up actions are to add a canary stage and automatic rollback (j.okafor), alert on the first post-deploy error-rate increase (t.kowalski), and document the rollback decision in the runbook (s.whitfield).

## Impact
Customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway for 12 minutes; service recovered. Eight alerts fired across the two components. The initial checkout-service SLO burn-rate alert reported an error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×); a subsequent checkout-service error-rate alert reported 0.09441 against 0.02. The alert data do not quantify affected customers or transactions.

## Detection
The first recorded incident alert was checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast at 2026-11-05T14:06:00Z, four minutes after its deploy, with error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147. Additional checkout-service and edge-gateway error-rate and latency alerts followed.

## Root cause
The incident commander's assessment identifies a faulty release to checkout-service (deploy 2026.11.05.2, change:chg-check-9247) as the root-cause component and change. Supporting references are the checkout-service error-rate metric, the deploy change, and a checkout-service NullPointerException log. The facts do not establish a more specific code-level mechanism.

### Contributing factors
- The checkout-service release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- There was no automatic rollback on error-rate regression.

## Timeline (virtual time, UTC)
- * `2026-11-05T14:02:00Z` [change] deploybot deployed checkout-service release 2026.11.05.2 (9 commits: express checkout address validation).
- * `2026-11-05T14:06:00Z` [detection] checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service error_rate_high fired: 0.09441 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_high fired: 659.54 ms versus threshold 400 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.07258 versus threshold 0.008.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway error_rate_high fired: 0.07104 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_high fired: 482.21 ms versus threshold 200 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:09:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_degraded fired: 670.48 ms versus threshold 300 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:10:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_degraded fired: 474.99 ms versus threshold 150 ms.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Posted a status update.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Rolled back the checkout-service deploy.
- * `2026-11-05T14:18:00Z` [recovery] checkout-service recovered.

## What went well
- The checkout-service burn-rate alert detected the regression four minutes after the deploy.
- The team posted a status update and rolled back checkout-service; recovery was recorded seven minutes after rollback.

## What went badly
- The release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- No automatic rollback was in place for an error-rate regression.

## Action items
- [p0] Add a canary stage and automatic rollback on error-rate regression for checkout-service - owner: j.okafor (prevent)
- [p1] Alert on the first error-rate increase after every checkout-service deploy - owner: t.kowalski (detect)
- [p2] Document the rollback decision in the checkout-service runbook - owner: s.whitfield (process)

## Lessons learned
- Check the deploy time against the first error-rate increase, then roll back only the component that changed.

# Postmortem INC-33721: INC-33721 (SEV2): checkout-service deploy caused checkout errors

*SEV2 - component `checkout-service` - revision 1 - approved*

## Summary
On November 5, INC-33721 was a 12-minute, customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway; eight alerts fired, including a checkout-service error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×). The incident commander identified the faulty checkout-service release as the root cause: it deployed at 14:02 UTC, the first alert fired at 14:06, a status update was posted and the deploy was rolled back at 14:11, and checkout-service recovered at 14:18; the specific code-level mechanism was not established. Follow-up actions are to add a canary stage and automatic rollback (j.okafor), alert on the first post-deploy error-rate increase (t.kowalski), and document the rollback decision in the runbook (s.whitfield).

## Impact
Customer-facing revenue-path incident affecting checkout-service and edge-gateway for 12 minutes; service recovered. Eight alerts fired across the two components. The initial checkout-service SLO burn-rate alert reported an error rate of 0.09281 against a 0.0147 threshold (6.31×); a subsequent checkout-service error-rate alert reported 0.09441 against 0.02. The alert data do not quantify affected customers or transactions.

## Detection
The first recorded incident alert was checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast at 2026-11-05T14:06:00Z, four minutes after its deploy, with error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147. Additional checkout-service and edge-gateway error-rate and latency alerts followed.

## Root cause
The incident commander's assessment identifies a faulty release to checkout-service (deploy 2026.11.05.2, change:chg-check-9247) as the root-cause component and change. Supporting references are the checkout-service error-rate metric, the deploy change, and a checkout-service NullPointerException log. The facts do not establish a more specific code-level mechanism.

### Contributing factors
- The checkout-service release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- There was no automatic rollback on error-rate regression.

## Timeline (virtual time, UTC)
- * `2026-11-05T14:02:00Z` [change] deploybot deployed checkout-service release 2026.11.05.2 (9 commits: express checkout address validation).
- * `2026-11-05T14:06:00Z` [detection] checkout-service slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.09281 versus threshold 0.0147.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service error_rate_high fired: 0.09441 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_high fired: 659.54 ms versus threshold 400 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:07:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway slo_burn_rate_fast fired: error_rate 0.07258 versus threshold 0.008.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway error_rate_high fired: 0.07104 versus threshold 0.02.
-   `2026-11-05T14:08:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_high fired: 482.21 ms versus threshold 200 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:09:00Z` [alert] checkout-service p95_latency_degraded fired: 670.48 ms versus threshold 300 ms.
-   `2026-11-05T14:10:00Z` [alert] edge-gateway p95_latency_degraded fired: 474.99 ms versus threshold 150 ms.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Posted a status update.
- * `2026-11-05T14:11:00Z` [action] Rolled back the checkout-service deploy.
- * `2026-11-05T14:18:00Z` [recovery] checkout-service recovered.

## What went well
- The checkout-service burn-rate alert detected the regression four minutes after the deploy.
- The team posted a status update and rolled back checkout-service; recovery was recorded seven minutes after rollback.

## What went badly
- The release reached all traffic without a canary stage.
- No automatic rollback was in place for an error-rate regression.

## Action items
- [p0] Add a canary stage and automatic rollback on error-rate regression for checkout-service - owner: j.okafor (prevent)
- [p1] Alert on the first error-rate increase after every checkout-service deploy - owner: t.kowalski (detect)
- [p2] Document the rollback decision in the checkout-service runbook - owner: s.whitfield (process)

## Lessons learned
- Check the deploy time against the first error-rate increase, then roll back only the component that changed.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

content.text:
The likely bottleneck is **pricing, reached through cart**, rather than checkout-service itself. Pricing’s p95 latency rose from roughly 210 ms to **1,376 ms** at 10:48, and its error rate reached **11.0%**. Cart then rose to **1,131 ms p95** with **8.9% errors**. The `new_pricing_engine` flag was raised from 0% to 50% at 10:42, shortly before pricing degraded at about 10:46. A pricing log also shows a tax-client timeout. That makes the flag rollout the leading suspect, **not a confirmed root cause**.

Checkout-service’s own latest p95 was **191 ms**, below its **400 ms SLO**. So the measured slowdown is in the cart/pricing path; I can’t yet say that checkout-service itself is slow. The nearby recommendation-service deploy is less consistent with the symptoms: its p95 remained near baseline, and it is not on checkout’s dependency path.

No change has been made. I’d have on-call review reverting the pricing flag, then verify pricing and cart recovery.

content.text:
The likely bottleneck is **pricing, reached through cart**, rather than checkout-service itself. Pricing’s p95 latency rose from roughly 210 ms to **1,376 ms** at 10:48, and its error rate reached **11.0%**. Cart then rose to **1,131 ms p95** with **8.9% errors**. The `new_pricing_engine` flag was raised from 0% to 50% at 10:42, shortly before pricing degraded at about 10:46. A pricing log also shows a tax-client timeout. That makes the flag rollout the leading suspect, **not a confirmed root cause**.

Checkout-service’s own latest p95 was **191 ms**, below its **400 ms SLO**. So the measured slowdown is in the cart/pricing path; I can’t yet say that checkout-service itself is slow. The nearby recommendation-service deploy is less consistent with the symptoms: its p95 remained near baseline, and it is not on checkout’s dependency path.

No change has been made. I’d have on-call review reverting the pricing flag, then verify pricing and cart recovery.

content.text:
The likely bottleneck is **pricing, reached through cart**, rather than checkout-service itself. Pricing’s p95 latency rose from roughly 210 ms to **1,376 ms** at 10:48, and its error rate reached **11.0%**. Cart then rose to **1,131 ms p95** with **8.9% errors**. The `new_pricing_engine` flag was raised from 0% to 50% at 10:42, shortly before pricing degraded at about 10:46. A pricing log also shows a tax-client timeout. That makes the flag rollout the leading suspect, **not a confirmed root cause**.

Checkout-service’s own latest p95 was **191 ms**, below its **400 ms SLO**. So the measured slowdown is in the cart/pricing path; I can’t yet say that checkout-service itself is slow. The nearby recommendation-service deploy is less consistent with the symptoms: its p95 remained near baseline, and it is not on checkout’s dependency path.

No change has been made. I’d have on-call review reverting the pricing flag, then verify pricing and cart recovery.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

agent_runs.summary: At 11:41 UTC, error rates rose simultaneously across all 11 queried services; by 11:49 they were 21.1–28.1%, versus baselines of 0.09–0.32%. Checkout p95 latency was 1,222 ms versus a 176 ms baseline, and auth p95 was 373 ms versus 59 ms; all 58 alerts listed remain firing. The synchronized, sustained impact favors a shared dependency or platform-level cause over an isolated checkout or auth failure, but these metric

In the 30-minute window, the first sustained failures began in cart-service at 11:42:37 UTC and auth-service at 11:43:18 UTC. After onset, the logs show 12 Redis connection timeouts, 12 “No route to host” errors across the event bus and orders DB, and 15 failed readiness probes, all associated with zone-b; before 11:42, the two services had only 8 scattered WARN+ entries combined. The simultaneous failures to differe

In the 240-minute window ending 11:49 UTC, there were **0 recorded changes across the 11 listed services**. Three changes occurred in other services between 10:46:54 and 10:52:54 UTC: a recommendation-service deploy, a catalog-service config change, and a search-service flag rollout from 0% to 5%. These do not directly support a change in the listed services as the trigger; without an incident onset time, their relev

Both services are tier 0, revenue-critical, and run in 2 zones. They share a synchronous dependency on sessions-cache, making it a plausible common-cause hypothesis; cart-service also depends on pricing-service, which would not directly explain auth-service degradation. Auth’s availability SLO is 99.99% (p95 200 ms), versus cart’s 99.95% (p95 300 ms); topology data provides no incident onset time or measured deviatio

Four similar incidents produced **34–66 alerts across 11 components in three minutes**; each was a zone-b network partition, not 11 separate service failures. That makes a shared zone failure a strong hypothesis for INC-54679, but the tools provided no live alert counts, onset time, zone breakdown, or baseline to confirm it; check whether alerts cluster by zone and minute before considering mitigation.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

Four similar incidents produced **34–66 alerts across 11 components in three minutes**; each was a zone-b network partition, not 11 separate service failures. agent_runs.summary: At 11:41 UTC, error rates rose simultaneously across all 11 queried services; by 11:49 they were 21.1–28.1%, versus baselines of 0.09–0.32%. Checkout p95 latency was 1,222 ms versus a 176 ms baseline, and auth p95 was 373 ms versus 59 ms; all 58 alerts listed remain firing. The synchronized, sustained impact favors a shared dependency or platform-level cause over an isolated checkout or auth failure, but these metric

In the 30-minute window, the first sustained failures began in cart-service at 11:42:37 UTC and auth-service at 11:43:18 UTC. After onset, the logs show 12 Redis connection timeouts, 12 “No route to host” errors across the event bus and orders DB, and 15 failed readiness probes, all associated with zone-b; before 11:42, the two services had only 8 scattered WARN+ entries combined. The simultaneous failures to differe

In the 240-minute window ending 11:49 UTC, there were **0 recorded changes across the 11 listed services**. Three changes occurred in other services between 10:46:54 and 10:52:54 UTC: a recommendation-service deploy, a catalog-service config change, and a search-service flag rollout from 0% to 5%. These do not directly support a change in the listed services as the trigger; without an incident onset time, their relev

Both services are tier 0, revenue-critical, and run in 2 zones. They share a synchronous dependency on sessions-cache, making it a plausible common-cause hypothesis; cart-service also depends on pricing-service, which would not directly explain auth-service degradation. Auth’s availability SLO is 99.99% (p95 200 ms), versus cart’s 99.95% (p95 300 ms); topology data provides no incident onset time or measured deviatio

Four similar incidents produced **34–66 alerts across 11 components in three minutes**; each was a zone-b network partition, not 11 separate service failures. That makes a shared zone failure a strong hypothesis for INC-54679, but the tools provided no live alert counts, onset time, zone breakdown, or baseline to confirm it; check whether alerts cluster by zone and minute before considering mitigation.

prefs.text: Commerce on-call wants a status update drafted for every SEV2 checkout incident, published only after the commander approves.
For pricing problems prefer reverting the feature flag over scaling out; scaling hides the slow call.
Never run kill_queries on orders-db without listing the longest sessions and their owners first.
DBA on-call must approve every index build; the SQL must use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
During the weekday 09:00-18:00 UTC freeze, platform prefers rollback over roll-forward for any bad deploy.
Keep incident narration terse: findings with numbers, no filler.
Always include the rollback command in the proposal summary.
Escalate to a human immediately when telemetry is flat or missing; do not act on guesses.
A single alert storm is one incident; open exactly one and attach the rest.
Shipping and inventory incidents never justify restarting the orders database.
Payments on-call prefers disabling the new-checkout flag over rolling back checkout-service; rollbacks need a 15 minute drain.

Checkout p95 latency was 1,222 ms versus a 176 ms baseline, and auth p95 was 373 ms versus 59 ms; all 58 alerts listed remain firing. The synchronized, sustained impact favors a shared dependency or platform-level cause over an isolated checkout or auth failure, but these metric

In the 30-minute window, the first sustained failures began in cart-service at 11:42:37 UTC and auth-service at 11:43:18 UTC. After onset, the logs show 12 Redis connection timeouts, 12 “No route to host” errors across the event bus and orders DB, and 15 failed readiness probes, all associated with zone-b; before 11:42, the two services had only 8 scattered WARN+ entries combined. The simultaneous failures to differe

In the 240-minute window ending 11:49 UTC, there were **0 recorded changes across the 11 listed services**. Three changes occurred in other services between 10:46:54 and 10:52:54 UTC: a recommendation-service deploy, a catalog-service config change, and a search-service flag rollout from 0% to 5%. These do not directly support a change in the listed services as the trigger; without an incident onset time, their relev

Both services are tier 0, revenue-critical, and run in 2 zones. They share a synchronous dependency on sessions-cache, making it a plausible common-cause hypothesis; cart-service also depends on pricing-service, which would not directly explain auth-service degradation. Auth’s availability SLO is 99.99% (p95 200 ms), versus cart’s 99.95% (p95 300 ms); topology data provides no incident onset time or measured deviatio

Four similar incidents produced **34–66 alerts across 11 components in three minutes**; each was a zone-b network partition, not 11 separate service failures. That makes a shared zone failure a strong hypothesis for INC-54679, but the tools provided no live alert counts, onset time, zone breakdown, or baseline to confirm it; check whether alerts cluster by zone and minute before considering mitigation.
